summary: Iraq lies on the Mesopotamian plain of West Asia, with the Tigris and Euphrates rivers flowing through it, and is the cradle of ancient civilizations such as Sumer and Babylon.

ranking.name: Islam (Shia)
ranking.description: Southern Iraq is one of the birthplaces of Shia Islam: the fourth caliph Ali is buried in Najaf, and his son Husayn was martyred at Karbala in 680. In the 18th–19th centuries, many nomadic tribes in the south converted to Shia Islam as they settled, making Shia the majority. But they were long excluded from power by Sunni rulers, and led the government only after Saddam Hussein's regime fell in 2003.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Both the Abbasid dynasty and the Ottoman Empire took Sunni Islam as orthodoxy, and Sunni Arabs were long Iraq's political and military elite; Saddam Hussein's regime was also centered on Sunnis. Sunnis are found mainly in the provinces west and north of Baghdad such as Anbar, Nineveh and Salahuddin, and most Kurds in the north are also Sunni.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Iraq is one of the oldest Christian regions in the world; the Chaldean Catholic Church and the Assyrian Church of the East can be traced back to the 1st–3rd centuries. Before 2003 there were over a million Christians, but post-war sectarian violence and the Islamic State's capture of Mosul and the Nineveh Plains in 2014 forced most to flee to the Kurdish region or abroad, and their numbers dropped sharply.

ranking.name: Yazidism
ranking.description: Yazidism is a Kurdish religion that blends ancient Iranian beliefs, Islamic Sufism and other elements; its holy site Lalish is in northern Iraq, and its followers are concentrated in the Sinjar mountains. They have historically been persecuted repeatedly, and in 2014 the Islamic State massacred Yazidis at Sinjar and abducted women, which the United Nations recognized as genocide.

religion.background: Mesopotamia, where Iraq lies, is the cradle of ancient civilizations such as Sumer and Babylon; Christianity arrived in the 1st–3rd centuries, and the Assyrian Church once flourished here. From 637 Arab Muslims conquered the region, and in 762 the Abbasid dynasty made Baghdad its capital, turning it into the center of the Islamic world. In 680 the third Imam, Husayn, was martyred at Karbala, making Najaf and Karbala holy cities of Shia Islam. Power was mostly held by Sunni elites under the Ottoman Empire, the monarchy after 1921, and Saddam Hussein's Ba'ath regime; after the US military overthrew Saddam in 2003, Shias gained political dominance, but sectarian conflict and the rise of the Islamic State in 2014 dealt heavy blows to Sunni regions and to minorities such as Christians and Yazidis.

language.official: Arabic and Kurdish are the official languages.

ranking.name: Arabic (Iraqi dialect)
ranking.description: After the Arab Muslim conquest in the 7th century, Arab tribes moved in and merged with the local Aramaic-speaking population, and Arabic gradually became the language of the majority. The Iraqi dialect (Mesopotamian Arabic) retains loanwords from Aramaic, Persian and Turkish, and is the national lingua franca and an official language.

ranking.name: Kurdish
ranking.description: The Kurds have lived since ancient times in the Zagros and Taurus mountain regions of the north. After the 1991 Gulf War the north gained autonomy, and the 2005 constitution established the Kurdistan Region and the official status of Kurdish. Kurdish is used in schools and government in Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Duhok and elsewhere, mainly in the Sorani and Kurmanji dialects.

ranking.name: Iraqi Turkmen
ranking.description: The ancestors of the Turkmen were Turkic tribes and soldiers who moved in during the Seljuk era in the 11th century and during the Ottoman period, and their language is close to Azerbaijani and Turkish. They live mainly in northern towns such as Kirkuk and Tal Afar, and the 2005 constitution recognizes Turkmen as an official language in their areas of concentration.

ranking.name: Neo-Aramaic
ranking.description: Aramaic was the lingua franca of the ancient Near East, and Assyrian and Chaldean Christians in northern Iraq still speak its modern forms (Neo-Aramaic, also called Sureth). Because of war and emigration, the number of speakers fell sharply in the 21st century, and they are now concentrated mainly in the Nineveh Plains and the Kurdish region.

language.history: The earliest languages used in the Iraq region were Sumerian and Akkadian; from the 1st millennium BCE Aramaic became the common language, and it survives to this day in the form of Neo-Aramaic in Christian communities. After the Arab conquest in the 7th century Arabic gradually replaced Aramaic, and Abbasid Baghdad even became the center of the Arabic scholarly translation movement. The Kurds of the northern mountains and the Turkmen who settled in the Ottoman period kept their own languages. The 2005 constitution made Arabic and Kurdish official languages side by side, and Turkmen and Aramaic (Syriac) also have official status in the areas where they are concentrated.

ranking.name: Masgouf (grilled fish)
ranking.description: A carp from the Tigris is split and laid flat, then slow-grilled on wooden stakes beside a charcoal fire, and served with tomato, onion and flatbread. The flesh has a wood-smoke aroma and is often seasoned with pickled mango sauce (amba) and lime.
ranking.history: Masgouf is regarded as Iraq's national dish, thanks to the abundant freshwater fish of the two rivers. The traditional method is to stand the fish beside a fire of burning apricot or tamarisk wood and grill it for hours; some scholars believe the technique goes back to ancient Mesopotamia. In the 20th century Abu Nuwas Street on Baghdad's Tigris riverbank became famous for its rows of grilled-fish restaurants, and eating grilled fish by the river on summer nights was part of Baghdadi life, but river pollution and war once caused the tradition to decline.

ranking.name: Dolma
ranking.description: Grape leaves, onions, eggplant, zucchini or bell peppers are stuffed with rice, minced meat and spices and stewed in a sour broth. The whole pot is turned out onto a platter when served, and tastes tangy, salty and appetizing.
ranking.history: The word dolma comes from the Turkish for "stuffed" and spread across the Middle East and the Balkans under Ottoman rule (16th–20th centuries). The Iraqi version is distinguished by stacking various vegetables together in the pot, with sourness from tomato and pomegranate molasses or lemon, and lamb ribs laid at the bottom. It is time-consuming and laborious, and is mostly wrapped by women together for Friday family meals or festivals.

ranking.name: Kleicha (date cookies)
ranking.description: Small round cookies filled with date paste or walnuts and sesame, flavored with cardamom and saffron. They are mostly round or rolled into patterns, with a crumbly, fragrant sweet texture, and are often served with tea.
ranking.history: Kleicha is often called Iraq's national pastry. Iraq produces abundant dates and has had a tradition of making sweets from dates since ancient times; some scholars link it to ritual pastries of ancient Mesopotamia, but details are hard to verify. Today Iraqi families bake large quantities of kleicha together before Eid al-Fitr to serve relatives and friends who come to pay festive visits, and Christians also make it at Christmas and Easter.

ranking.name: Quzi (roast lamb with rice)
ranking.description: A whole lamb or leg of lamb is slow-roasted until tender and laid over rice cooked with nuts, raisins and spices. The portion is huge, and the whole platter is usually served for many people to share.
ranking.history: Quzi comes from the guest-hosting tradition of the Bedouin of the Arabian Peninsula and Mesopotamia, in which serving a whole lamb to guests is a way for nomadic societies to show generosity. In Iraq it often appears at large banquets for weddings, funerals and religious holidays, and is also one of the foods people give out to the public during Ashura (commemorating Husayn's martyrdom) among Shias.

ranking.name: Kubba
ranking.description: Dumplings with a shell made of crushed wheat or rice and minced meat, filled with a meat stuffing and then deep-fried or boiled; the Mosul version is especially large and flat. The shell is crisp and the filling juicy, and it can be eaten as a snack or used as a soup ingredient.
ranking.history: Kubba is found throughout the Middle East (called kibbeh in Lebanon), and Iraqis have developed many variations: the large disc-shaped kubba of Mosul in the north, the rice-shell kubba of Baghdad, and kubba hamudh served in a sour soup. After large numbers of Iraqi Jews emigrated to Israel in the mid-20th century, they also brought kubba soup to Jerusalem, where it became a popular local dish.
